summary.text: 花 means “flower” and is constructed as a phonosemantic character: 艹 marks the plant category, while 化 provides a similar-sounding cue. Tang citations attest the flower and “to flower” uses; the graph’s first appearance is unresolved.

formation.text: The later graph combines a plant-category element, 艹, with 化 as a probable sound element. Mandarin huā and huà are similar, and Old Chinese reconstructions also show a partial sound match, though they do not directly record ancient speech or date the graph’s formation.

components.text: 艹 is the plant-category element in 花. It is a conventional side form of 艸, not evidence here of a separate historical stage.

化 serves as a probable sound element in 花. Mandarin 花 huā and 化 huà are similar but differ in tone and vowel; Baxter–Sagart reconstructions share a similar onset and medial sequence but differ in their ending.

sound.text: Mandarin 花 huā and 化 huà are similar, though their tones and vowels differ.

In Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese reconstructions, 花 *qʷʰˤra and 化 *qʷʰˤ<r>aj-s share a similar onset and medial sequence but differ in the ending. These are reconstructed forms, not direct records of ancient speech.

history.text: A modern seal-script-style drawing presents 花 in a later script style; it is not an ancient artifact or a dated step in the graph’s development.

The received Shuowen analysis treats 𠌶 as the flower of grasses and trees, composed of 𠂹 and phonetic 亏, and 華 as flourishing, composed of 艸 and 𠌶. A modern paleographic proposal instead sees a plant and flower in early 𠌶 and 于 as its sound element, suggesting that later graphic alteration made the flower strokes resemble 𠂹. These analyses conflict, and neither establishes a continuous graphic sequence into 花.

Dictionaries describe 花 as a later form associated with 華 and using 化 for sound. Tang citations attest 花 in use, but the date when this graph arose and its precise graphic connection with 𠌶 or 華 remain unresolved.

uncertainties.text: The supplied evidence identifies no oracle-bone form or primary dated first occurrence of 花. The seal-style drawing does not establish the graph’s earliest formation.

化 is a plausible sound element, supported by component analyses and reconstructed comparisons. Those comparisons are not ancient recordings and do not establish when 花 was formed or its exact original pronunciation.
The received Shuowen analysis of 𠌶 conflicts with a modern proposal that it depicts a plant and flower and contains phonetic 于; the graphic history remains disputed.

senses.period: Tang citations; earlier first use of 花 unresolved
senses.text: Tang citations attest 花 for the noun “flower.” The older graphs 𠌶 and 華 have flower-related definitions or reported uses, but those do not establish an early attestation of 花 itself.
A Tang citation attests 花 as a verb meaning “to flower.” The evidence does not establish when this use arose relative to the noun.

senses.gloss: flower-like objects and other figurative or extended senses
senses.text: Later recorded senses include flower-like objects, beauty, patterns, and expenditure. Their dates and paths of development from “flower” are unresolved.

developments.text: Both noun and verb uses are attested, but the evidence does not establish that one developed from the other or show their chronology.

limitations.text: The first use of 花 as a graph is unresolved, as are the chronology of the noun and verb uses and the semantic paths to later figurative meanings.

overview.text: 花 means “flower.” 艹 marks the plant category, while 化 offers a similar-sounding cue. Tang citations attest this graph, but its first appearance is unresolved.

components.text: 艹 points to the plant category associated with flowers.
化 offers a sound cue; 花 and 化 are similar in Mandarin and in one set of Old Chinese reconstructions.

relationships.text: 艹 contributes the plant category in 花’s phonosemantic construction.
化 is a proposed sound element in 花. Similar readings support the analysis, although reconstructions neither record ancient speech directly nor date the graph.
Dictionaries describe 花 as a later form or variant associated with 華, but the evidence does not establish a continuous graphic sequence between them.
